summary: This RFC defines the Heartbeat Extension for TLS and DTLS. It adds a keep-alive protocol that avoids renegotiation and provides a basis for path MTU discovery in DTLS. The extension later became widely known because of a serious implementation bug in a popular library.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6520 adds heartbeat messages to TLS and DTLS. One endpoint can send a request and check that the peer replies with the same payload, or use a padded request to probe the path size for DTLS.

questions: what is the heartbeat in tls
what is the tls heartbeat extension
subtitle: A TLS and DTLS message for checking whether a peer is reachable and probing the path MTU.

tldr.problem: TLS and DTLS lacked a simple way to check that a peer remained reachable without renegotiating or sending continuous application data.
tldr.mechanism: The extension defines a request carrying a payload and random padding; the peer answers with a response containing an exact copy of that payload.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can check liveness, refresh NAT state and use padded DTLS requests as path-MTU probes. RFC 6520 was updated by RFC 8447.

today: RFC 6520 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It has been updated by RFC 8447.

sections.title: Why the Heartbeat Extension Exists
sections.content:
DTLS protects traffic over unreliable transports, which often do not manage sessions. Before this extension, checking whether a DTLS peer was alive could require renegotiation. DTLS also needed a way to probe the path maximum transmission unit without interrupting user messages.

TLS runs over reliable transports, but a connection may have no data to send continuously. The Heartbeat Extension adds a request that the peer answers, providing a keep-alive mechanism without renegotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: A secure connection may be quiet even while both endpoints are working. A heartbeat request lets one endpoint check whether the other can still reply.

sections.title: Agreeing to Receive Heartbeats
sections.content:
Each endpoint advertises a HeartbeatMode in a Hello extension. peer_allowed_to_send means it will accept requests and answer them. peer_not_allowed_to_send means it only wants to send requests, not receive them.

An endpoint must not send a request to a peer that chose peer_not_allowed_to_send. A peer that receives a prohibited request should silently drop it and may send an unexpected_message alert. An unknown mode requires an illegal_parameter alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint says whether it will answer heartbeat requests. A sender must respect a peer that has said it will not receive them.

sections.title: Request and Response Behavior
sections.content:
Heartbeat runs over the TLS or DTLS Record Layer and has two message types: heartbeat_request and heartbeat_response. A request should be answered unless another rule prohibits it. Requests should not be sent during a handshake, and DTLS requests from older epochs should be discarded.

Only one request may be in flight at a time. Over an unreliable transport such as UDP, the request is retransmitted using DTLS's timeout scheme; after repeated unanswered attempts, the connection should be terminated. Over a reliable transport such as TCP, it is sent once and the application may end the connection if no reply arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint sends one request at a time and waits for its matching reply. On an unreliable transport it retries; on a reliable transport the transport handles retransmission.

sections.title: Heartbeat Message Contents
sections.content:
A message contains a one-byte type, a two-byte payload length, the payload and padding. The total message length must not exceed 2^14 or the negotiated max_fragment_length. Padding contains random data, must be at least 16 bytes, and must be ignored by the receiver.

A receiver answering a request must copy the request payload exactly into the response. If the payload length is too large for the received message, the message is silently discarded. A response with the wrong payload is also discarded; a matching response stops the retransmission timer.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a payload and random padding. The peer copies the payload exactly into its reply and ignores the padding.

sections.title: Liveness Checks and Path-MTU Probes
sections.content:
Heartbeat requests work in each direction independently; an endpoint should not assume its peer will also send them. For DTLS path-MTU discovery, padded requests serve as probe packets.

For a liveness check, a request confirms that the peer is reachable and can refresh Network Address Translator state. The RFC recommends sending it only after an idle period of at least multiple round-trip times. That period should be configurable from one second to multiple minutes and tunable for each peer.
sections.plainLanguage: A padded DTLS request can test the path size. A request after an idle period can also check reachability and refresh address-translation state.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that the security considerations of the TLS and DTLS specifications apply. It states that the Heartbeat Extension introduces no new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC relies on the security rules of TLS and DTLS. It states that this extension adds no new security considerations.
